advances: Refutes the proposed absolute-constant entropy-to-original-cap inequality, even for uniform complete globally extendable tables and the explicit globally strongly convex cost \(F(x)=\|x\|^2\). The obstruction survives every other strictly convex choice of \(F\), so an adaptive choice of the cost cannot repair this consumer on these tables. Every original source capacity is retained, and the original integral hitting score is computed exactly at every center and cutoff. This is a counterexample to the registered numerical consumer, not to the locked weak Oertel conjecture.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The complete-support geometry, global extension, whole-face selection, and exact original-cap computations are proved above. The two declared accepted inputs supply only the canonical definitions and normalization conventions used here.
proof:
We first verify the complete lattice support without omitting any boundary site. For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), write \(s=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\). The unique barycentric coefficients of \(x\) with respect to the displayed simplex vertices are

\[
\lambda_0=\frac{1-s}{n+1},\qquad
\lambda_i=x_i+\frac{1-s}{n+1}\quad(1\le i\le n).
\]

Indeed, their sum is one and \(x_i=\lambda_i-\lambda_0\). These identities also prove uniqueness and affine independence of the vertices. Thus \(x\in P\) if and only if \(s\le1\) and \(x_i\ge(s-1)/(n+1)\) for every \(i\).

Every coordinate of a point of \(P\) is at least \(-1\), because every vertex has that property. If \(x\in P\cap\mathbb Z^n\), then \(-n\le s\le1\), with \(s\) integral. When \(s=-n\), the coordinate bounds \(x_i\ge-1\) force every coordinate to equal \(-1\), giving \(x=\mathbf v_0\). When \(-n+1\le s\le0\), the inequality \((s-1)/(n+1)>-1\) and integrality force \(x_i\ge0\) for every \(i\). Hence negative \(s\) in this range is impossible, and \(s=0\) forces \(x=\mathbf0\). When \(s=1\), all coordinates are nonnegative integers summing to one, so \(x\) is one of \(\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_n\). Conversely every point of \(D\) is in \(P\), since \(\sum_{i=0}^n\mathbf v_i=\mathbf0\) and the origin is the average of the vertices. This proves \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n=D\).

The prescribed probabilities sum to one. The function equal to \(1/(n+2)\) on the closed convex set \(P\) and zero outside \(P\) is a finite-valued globally log-concave extension agreeing with every lattice value, including all lattice zeros, in the convention of `488f0a583886b5fc`. If both endpoints are in \(P\), their convex combination is in \(P\) and the extension inequality holds with equality. If either endpoint is outside, its right side is zero. This verifies the table hypotheses and the stated original normalization directly. In particular every original logarithmic barycentric cost \(G_E\) is zero.

We next verify selection on the entire minimizing face for an arbitrary strictly convex \(F\), rather than assuming any row theorem beyond its accepted range. The source mean is \(\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}p_{\mathbf I}\mathbf I=\mathbf0\). For any feasible array in the definition of `c300e9d112cefeb0`, summing the column identities and row moment identities gives \(\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}=1\) and \(\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}\mathbf J=\mathbf0\). Strict convexity and Jensen's inequality therefore imply

\[
V_F(r)=\sum_{\mathbf J\in D}q_{\mathbf J}F(\mathbf J)
\ge F(\mathbf0),
\]

with equality only when the target law is concentrated at \(\mathbf0\). To see the equality condition explicitly, a law supported at one site has mean equal to that site, so its mean is zero only at the origin. If at least two distinct sites have positive mass, the strict Jensen inequality gives a strictly larger value than \(F(\mathbf0)\).

The array displayed in the statement is feasible: its column sums equal \(p\), its sole nonzero row has total mass one and mean zero, and every zero row satisfies its moment identity. It attains \(F(\mathbf0)\). Thus every minimizing array has zero row mass at every nonzero target. Nonnegativity makes all entries of those rows zero; the original column equations then force \(r_{\mathbf0,\mathbf I}=p_{\mathbf I}\) for every source. The whole minimizing face is consequently the asserted singleton, for every strictly convex \(F\). Entropy selection on that entire face is exactly this array. The selected row is the unchanged globally extendable original law, with complete support \(D\), and its only nonzero assignment share at each source is one. It follows directly from the definitions that \(S(q_F)=H(r_F)=0\). Since the original potential is zero at all sites, the original energy \(G_F\) is also zero.

It remains to compute the original integral score, including every center and cutoff. At a vertex \(\mathbf v_i\), extremality means that its only positive barycentric representation on an affinely independent support is the singleton \(\{\mathbf v_i\}\). Hence its original family \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf v_i}\) in `488f0a583886b5fc` has exactly this one member. Any hitting set must contain that original source and the singleton itself is a hitting set, giving \(m_{\log}(\mathbf v_i,L;p)=1/(n+2)\) for every \(L\ge0\).

At \(\mathbf0\), the original family has exactly two members: \(\{\mathbf0\}\) and \(\{\mathbf v_0,\ldots,\mathbf v_n\}\). Here is a complete verification. Any nonnegative coefficients satisfying \(\sum_{i=0}^n a_i\mathbf v_i=\mathbf0\) obey \(a_i=a_0\) for each \(1\le i\le n\), by comparing coordinates. Thus a positive representation of the origin using nonzero sites must use every vertex, and its normalized coefficients are all \(1/(n+1)\). A positive representation involving the origin and at least one vertex must likewise include every vertex; that support has \(n+2\) sites and is affinely dependent, so it is excluded from \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf0}\). The singleton and the full vertex simplex both have the required positive coefficients and affine independence. This exhausts the family.

All costs are zero, so every cutoff \(L\ge0\) contains the full family just identified. A hitting set at the origin must contain the origin and at least one original vertex, and these two sources suffice. Their original weights give \(m_{\log}(\mathbf0,L;p)=2/(n+2)\). No row normalization, proportional amplification, fractional certificate, or deletion of original sources enters this calculation.

The closed-cap characterization of `488f0a583886b5fc` also realizes these values with admissible normals. At \(\mathbf0\), take \(t=0\) and \(\mathbf b=(n,-1,\ldots,-1)\). Its original atom scores are \(n\) at \(\mathbf v_1\), \(-1\) at every other vertex, and zero at \(\mathbf0\). Its closed cap consequently contains exactly \(\{\mathbf0,\mathbf v_1\}\), with the equality atom \(\mathbf0\) retained. At \(\mathbf v_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\), take \(t=0\) and \(\mathbf b=\mathbf e_i\); its closed cap through that target contains just \(\mathbf v_i\). At \(\mathbf v_0\), take \(t=0\) and \(\mathbf b=(-1,\ldots,-1)\); its closed cap likewise contains just \(\mathbf v_0\). These statements include \(n=1\).

These normals are admissible at every \(L\ge0\). More generally, because \(\phi\) vanishes, the canonical cap score is \(\mathbf b\cdot(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)+tL\). For \(\mathbf b\ne\mathbf0\), increasing the nonnegative offset \(tL\) cannot remove any atom from the corresponding \(t=0\) closed cap. For \(\mathbf b=\mathbf0\), the admissible normal has \(t>0\), and all atoms belong to its cap, including when \(L=0\). Equivalently, every canonical closed cap hits the original families already computed. Thus neither positive \(t\), equality atoms, nor any cutoff creates a smaller original cap mass.

At each center the mass is constant in \(L\), so the maximum of its ratio with \(1+L\) occurs at \(L=0\). Maximizing over all the complete original centers yields \(\mathcal B_{\log}^{\mathrm{hit}}(p)=2/(n+2)\).

Finally, on every member of this exact family the proposed right side is \(c\), since \(S(q_F)=H(r_F)=G_F=0\). Given any \(c>0\), choose an integer \(n\ge1\) with \(n+2>2/c\). The computed score is then strictly less than \(c\), contradicting the proposed inequality. This applies even if \(F\) is chosen adaptively after seeing the original table, because all finite strictly convex choices have the same unique minimizing array here. These arrays also satisfy any upper energy bound of the stated form \(G_F\le K[n\log2-S(q_F)+H(r_F)]\) with an arbitrary scalar coefficient \(K>0\), since its left side is zero. That additional energy condition therefore does not repair the false consumer.

For clarity about the locked target, the elementary induction \(2^n\ge n+1\) for \(n\ge0\) gives \(2^{n+1}\ge2n+2\ge n+2\) for \(n\ge1\). Thus the exact normalized dyadic score \(2^{n+1}/(n+2)\) is at least one. The counterexample establishes failure of the stronger entropy consumer while retaining a score at least \(2^{-n}W\); it supplies no disproof of the locked conjecture.
statement:
Use the original logarithmic hitting definitions of accepted fact `488f0a583886b5fc` and the feasible arrays, entire minimizing faces, entropy selection, and original-potential energy of accepted fact `c300e9d112cefeb0`. All logarithms are natural.

For each integer \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_n\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb R^n\), put \(\mathbf v_0=(-1,\ldots,-1)\), and put \(\mathbf v_i=\mathbf e_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\). Define

\[
\begin{aligned}
P&=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf v_0,\ldots,\mathbf v_n\},\\
D&=\{\mathbf0,\mathbf v_0,\ldots,\mathbf v_n\},\\
p_{\mathbf I}&=\frac1{n+2}\quad(\mathbf I\in D),\qquad
p_{\mathbf I}=0\quad(\mathbf I\notin D).
\end{aligned}
\]

This is a complete globally extendable probability table: \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n=D\). The exact normalization to `488f0a583886b5fc` is \(w=p\), \(W=1\), \(w_{\max}=1/(n+2)\), \(\phi_{\mathbf I}=0\) at every original source, and \(B=0\).

Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be any finite strictly convex function; in particular one may choose the explicit globally strongly convex function \(F(x)=\|x\|^2\). In the notation of `c300e9d112cefeb0`, the entire \(V_F\)-minimizing face is the singleton array

\[
r_{F,\mathbf J,\mathbf I}=
\begin{cases}
p_{\mathbf I},&\mathbf J=\mathbf0,\ \mathbf I\in D,\\
0,&\mathbf J\ne\mathbf0,\ \mathbf I\in D.
\end{cases}
\]

Consequently \(q_F\) is the unit mass at \(\mathbf0\), \(S(q_F)=0\), \(H(r_F)=0\), and \(G_F=0\). Here \(H(r_F)\) is the conditional assignment entropy, whereas the original source entropy is \(-\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}p_{\mathbf I}\log p_{\mathbf I}=\log(n+2)\). For every real \(L\ge0\), with all original source capacities unchanged,

\[
\begin{aligned}
m_{\log}(\mathbf0,L;p)&=\frac2{n+2},\\
m_{\log}(\mathbf v_i,L;p)&=\frac1{n+2}\quad(0\le i\le n),\\
\mathcal B_{\log}^{\mathrm{hit}}(p)&=\frac2{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The normalized dyadic score nevertheless satisfies \(2^n\mathcal B_{\log}^{\mathrm{hit}}(p)=2^{n+1}/(n+2)\ge1\), so these tables pass the locked dyadic scale. There is no absolute \(c>0\) for which all the tables and entropy-selected arrays in the registered subgoal satisfy

\[
\mathcal B_{\log}^{\mathrm{hit}}(p)
\ge c\exp(-S(q_F))\frac{1+H(r_F)}{1+G_F}.
\]
